lesson.title: Leases: how lessees and lessors put them in the financial statements
lesson.summary: A lease lets one company use an asset owned by another in return for payments. This lesson shows how the user (lessee) and the owner (lessor) record that deal under US GAAP and IFRS, and why the choice changes leverage, expenses and cash flow categories.

sections.heading: Leasing is renting with a long horizon
sections.body_markdown: A **lease** is a contract giving one party (the **lessee**) the right to use an asset for a set period in return for payments to the owner (the **lessor**). Renting a flat is the everyday version. For companies, the accounting question is whether the deal is really just a rental or is closer to borrowing money to buy the asset. Accounting follows the economic substance of the contract rather than its legal wording. Years ago, many big leases stayed off the balance sheet and acted as hidden debt. Current standards (IFRS 16 and US GAAP ASC 842) bring most leases onto the lessee's balance sheet.

sections.heading: The lessee's view
sections.body_markdown:
At the start of a lease, a lessee records two things:

- a **lease liability**: the present value (today's value) of the remaining lease payments, discounted at the rate implicit in the lease if known, otherwise the lessee's incremental borrowing rate (what it would pay to borrow similar money)
- a **right-of-use (ROU) asset**: roughly the same amount, plus any initial direct costs and prepayments, less incentives

**IFRS 16** has a single lessee model. Almost every lease is treated like a purchase financed by a loan. The income statement shows **depreciation** of the ROU asset plus **interest** on the liability. Interest is largest at the start because the liability is largest then, so total expense is **front-loaded**.

**US GAAP** keeps two lessee categories. A **finance lease** looks like the IFRS pattern (amortization plus interest). An **operating lease** still puts an ROU asset and liability on the balance sheet, but the income statement shows one **straight-line lease expense**.

Under both frameworks a lessee may skip balance-sheet recognition for **short-term leases** (12 months or less). IFRS also allows a **low-value asset** exemption, chosen lease by lease. US GAAP has no low-value exemption.

sections.heading: The lessor's view
sections.body_markdown:
The lessor must decide whether it has effectively sold or financed the asset, or merely rented it out.

- **Operating lease**: the lessor keeps the asset on its balance sheet, depreciates it, and records **rental income**, typically straight-line.
- **Finance lease** (IFRS) or **sales-type / direct financing lease** (US GAAP): the lessor removes the asset and records a **lease receivable**, which is like a loan balance. Each payment is split into interest income (opening receivable × implicit rate) and principal repayment.

If the lessor is a manufacturer or dealer, it can show a **selling profit** (revenue minus the asset's carrying cost) when the lease starts. Under US GAAP, selling profit on a *direct financing* lease is deferred and spread over the lease, whereas a sales-type lease recognizes it at commencement. Under IFRS, selling profit on a finance lease is recognized at commencement.

Lessors classify at inception, based on whether substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership pass to the lessee.

sections.heading: Why it matters for analysis and cash flows
sections.body_markdown:
Recognizing the liability raises reported debt and lowers solvency ratios, even though the company's cash commitments have not changed. Early-year expense is higher under the IFRS/finance-lease pattern, so reported profit is lower early and higher later.

Cash-flow presentation also differs. Under IFRS, the **principal** part of a lessee's payment is in **financing** activities. The **interest** part can go in operating or financing, depending on the company's policy. Under US GAAP, a finance lease puts principal in financing and interest in operating. An operating lease puts the whole payment in operating cash flow. Cash paid is the same in total; only the labels move, which affects CFO comparisons.

worked_example.problem: A lessee signs a 5-year equipment lease, with no exemption available. It pays 10,000 at the end of each year. The rate implicit in the lease is not known, so the lessee uses its incremental borrowing rate of 6% per year. There are no initial direct costs, incentives or prepayments. Under IFRS 16, find (a) the initial lease liability and ROU asset, and (b) total income statement expense in year 1 using straight-line depreciation and no residual value.
steps: Set the calculator for end-of-period payments: 2ND BGN, check the display shows END, then 2ND SET and 2ND QUIT. Clear the TVM registers with 2ND CLR TVM.
Enter N = 5, I/Y = 6, PMT = −10,000, FV = 0. Press CPT PV. The result is 42,123.64, the initial lease liability.
The ROU asset starts at the same amount, 42,123.64, because there are no other costs or incentives.
Year-1 total expense = 2,527.42 + 8,424.73 = 10,952.15. This is above the 10,000 cash payment, which shows the front-loading.
worked_example.answer: Initial lease liability = ROU asset ≈ 42,123.64. Year-1 expense ≈ 10,952.15 (interest 2,527.42 + depreciation 8,424.73), versus a 10,000 payment. Closing liability ≈ 34,651.06.

formulas.name: Initial lease liability
formulas.where: L_0 = lease liability at commencement; P_t = lease payment at time t; r = discount rate per period (implicit rate if known, otherwise incremental borrowing rate); n = number of payments.

formulas.name: Interest on the lease liability (or receivable)
formulas.where: L_{t-1} = opening balance of the lease liability (lessee) or lease receivable (lessor) for period t; r = periodic rate used at commencement.

formulas.name: Straight-line ROU depreciation
formulas.where: ROU asset = right-of-use asset at commencement; residual = expected value at the end (often zero for a lessee); lease term = number of periods over which the asset is depreciated.

formulas.name: Level lease payment to earn a target rate
formulas.where: PV = amount the lessor invests (asset fair value, with no residual); r = implicit rate per period; n = number of payments in arrears; PMT = level payment.

exam_traps: Treating an IFRS lessee lease as one level rent expense. Under IFRS 16 the lessee reports depreciation plus interest, so expense is higher in early years.
Thinking a US GAAP operating lease stays off the balance sheet. It does not: the lessee records an ROU asset and lease liability, and only the income statement shows a single straight-line expense.
Mixing up payment timing. Payments at the start of each period (annuity due) give a larger present value than payments at the end. Check the timing before using the calculator.
Applying lessee labels to lessors. The lessor's choice is operating versus finance (IFRS) or sales-type / direct financing (US GAAP). Only an operating lessor keeps the asset and depreciates it.
Assuming the low-value exemption exists under both frameworks. It exists only under IFRS; the 12-month short-term exemption exists under both.

mcqs.stem: A lessee signs a 4-year lease with payments of 20,000 at the end of each year. Its discount rate is 8% per year, compounded annually, and no recognition exemption applies. What is the initial lease liability, rounded to the nearest cent?

options.explanation: This treats the payments as made at the start of each year (annuity due), which inflates the present value by a factor of 1.08. The stem says end of year.
This simply adds up the payments (4 × 20,000) without discounting. The liability is a present value, not the total cash.

mcqs.stem: A company is the lessee in a 5-year equipment lease with no exemption available. Under IFRS 16, which description best fits the income statement effect?

options.text: Depreciation of the ROU asset plus interest on the lease liability, with total expense higher in the early years
options.explanation: Correct. IFRS 16 has a single lessee model, like a financed purchase. Interest is largest when the liability is largest, so total expense is front-loaded.

options.text: One equal rent expense each year, matching the cash payment and unaffected by the lease balance
options.explanation: This is the old operating-lease pattern, or the US GAAP operating-lease presentation. IFRS 16 does not allow it for a lessee.

options.text: Interest expense only, because the lessee does not own the asset and so records no depreciation
options.explanation: This ignores the ROU asset. The lessee recognizes an asset and depreciates it over the shorter of the lease term or its useful life, unless ownership transfers.

mcqs.stem: Under US GAAP, a lessee has a long-term lease that is classified as an operating lease. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The lease stays off the balance sheet and the payments are expensed as rent when paid, with no liability
options.explanation: This is the pre-2019 treatment. ASC 842 requires most operating leases to be recognized on the lessee's balance sheet.

options.text: The income statement shows depreciation and interest separately, just as it does for a finance lease
options.explanation: This is the finance-lease presentation. Operating leases under US GAAP do not split the expense into depreciation and interest.

options.text: An ROU asset and lease liability are recognized, and one straight-line lease expense is reported in operating activities
options.explanation: Correct. The balance sheet effect is similar to a finance lease, but the income statement shows a single straight-line expense, and all cash payments are operating.

mcqs.stem: A lessor buys equipment for 100,000 and leases it under a finance lease with no residual value. It wants to earn an implicit rate of 5% per year, compounded annually, from 6 equal annual payments made at the end of each year. What is the level annual payment, rounded to the nearest cent?

options.explanation: This assumes payments at the start of each year (annuity due), which lowers the payment. The stem says end of year.
This divides 100,000 by 6 and ignores interest. The payments must also earn the 5% implicit return.

mcqs.stem: A lessor leases a machine and classifies the lease as an operating lease. Which statement about the lessor's accounting is correct?

options.text: It removes the machine and records a lease receivable equal to the present value of the lease payments
options.explanation: This describes a finance (or sales-type) lease. An operating lessor does not derecognize the asset.

options.text: It keeps the machine on its balance sheet, depreciates it, and records rental income over the lease
options.explanation: Correct. In an operating lease the risks and rewards of ownership stay with the lessor, so it keeps and depreciates the asset and records rental income.

options.text: It recognizes a selling profit at commencement and then earns interest income on a lease receivable
options.explanation: This is manufacturer/dealer finance (sales-type) accounting, not operating-lease accounting.

mcqs.stem: A lessee signs a 5-year lease with payments of 12,000 at the beginning of each year (the first payment is made at commencement). Its discount rate is 7% per year, compounded annually, and no exemption applies. What is the initial lease liability, rounded to the nearest cent?

options.explanation: Correct. Payments are in advance, so use an annuity due: 12,000 × 4.10020 × 1.07 = 52,646.54. This is the same as the first payment plus the PV of four end-of-year payments.
This treats the payments as end-of-year (ordinary annuity) and ignores that the first payment is made at commencement.
This adds the five payments without discounting. The liability is the present value of the payments.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about lessee recognition exemptions is correct?

options.text: Only US GAAP allows a low-value asset exemption, and IFRS offers none
options.explanation: This reverses the frameworks. IFRS 16 has a low-value exemption (chosen lease by lease); US GAAP does not.

options.text: Neither framework exempts short-term leases, and only low-value assets can be kept off the balance sheet
options.explanation: Both frameworks allow an exemption for leases of 12 months or less, so short-term leases can stay off the balance sheet.

options.text: Both allow a short-term (12 months or less) exemption, but only IFRS has a low-value asset exemption
options.explanation: Correct. ASC 842 has no recognition exemption based on the asset's value. IFRS 16 lets lessees elect it lease by lease.

mcqs.stem: A lessee reports under IFRS and has a 5-year equipment lease recognized on its balance sheet. In the statement of cash flows, the principal portion of each lease payment is most likely classified as:

options.text: operating activities, because it replaces the rent that was previously expensed
options.explanation: This is the old operating-lease habit. Under IFRS the principal repayment of the lease liability is a financing cash flow.

options.text: financing activities, because it repays the liability recognized to fund use of the asset
options.explanation: Correct. Under IFRS the principal portion is financing. The interest portion can be operating or financing, depending on the company's policy.

options.text: investing activities, because the payments relate to acquiring the right to use an asset
options.explanation: This confuses the ROU asset with a purchase of PP&E. The cash outflow is repayment of a lease liability, so it is financing, not investing.

flashcards.front: What two items does a lessee record at the start of a lease (no exemption)?
flashcards.back: A right-of-use (ROU) asset and a lease liability, the liability being the present value of the lease payments at the implicit rate (if known) or the incremental borrowing rate.

flashcards.front: How does the lessee's income statement differ between IFRS 16 leases and US GAAP operating leases?
flashcards.back: IFRS 16 shows ROU depreciation plus interest, with expense front-loaded. A US GAAP operating lease shows one straight-line lease expense. A US GAAP finance lease follows the IFRS pattern.

flashcards.front: How does a lessor account for an operating lease versus a finance lease?
flashcards.back: Operating: keeps and depreciates the asset and records rental income. Finance (IFRS) / sales-type or direct financing (US GAAP): derecognizes the asset, records a lease receivable and earns interest income.

flashcards.front: Which lessee recognition exemptions exist, and under which framework?
flashcards.back: Short-term leases (12 months or less) under both frameworks; low-value assets under IFRS only.
